panels.description: The cluster's overall operating state: INITIALIZING while starting up, RUNNING in normal operation, PAUSED when transactions are held (for example during maintenance), or SHUTTINGDOWN. Anything other than RUNNING means the cluster is not serving traffic normally.
panels.title: State

panels.description: Whether the cluster still has its full set of redundant partition copies (FULL) or has lost one or more and is running with reduced redundancy (REDUCED). REDUCED means a further node failure is more likely to cause data loss or an outage.
panels.title: Safety

panels.description: The number of servers currently up and part of the cluster. Compare this with the configured full size to see whether any nodes are missing.
panels.title: Live nodes

panels.description: The number of servers the cluster is configured to run with. If fewer nodes are live than this, some servers are down or have not yet rejoined.
panels.title: Full size

panels.description: The configured K-safety factor: how many redundant copies of each partition the cluster keeps. A K-factor of 1, for example, lets the cluster survive one server failure without losing data.
panels.title: K-factor

panels.description: The number of partitions (execution sites) each server runs. Together with the node count this determines how the workload is spread across the cluster.
panels.title: Sites/host

panels.description: How long the cluster has been running since it was last started. A recent, unexpected reset of this value indicates the cluster restarted.
panels.title: Uptime

panels.description: The VoltDB software version the cluster is running. Useful for confirming an upgrade completed and that all nodes report the same version.
panels.title: Version

panels.description: A per-node summary of the cluster: each node's current load, memory and heap usage against their limits, throughput (including the fan-out to partition replicas), 95th-percentile initiator latency (full request-to-response time), uptime, version, and whether it is ready for cross-datacenter replication (XDCR). Use it to spot nodes that are overloaded, on the wrong version, or recently restarted.
panels.title: Nodes

panels.description: The largest clock difference right now between any two servers in the cluster. Large clock skew can disrupt coordination between nodes, so this should stay small.
panels.title: Clock skew

panels.description: The total number of client connection attempts that were refused because the server had already reached its connection limit. Any nonzero value means clients were unable to connect.
panels.title: Dropped

panels.description: How much client-connection capacity remains before the server reaches its configured connection limit. A low value warns that the server is close to refusing new client connections.
panels.title: Free conns

panels.description: How many file descriptors the server process can still open before hitting its operating-system limit. Running out of file descriptors causes connections and file operations to fail.
panels.title: FD usage

panels.description: The maximum number of file descriptors the server process is allowed to open. If this ceiling is set too low, the server can run out under heavy connection or file load.
panels.title: FD limit

panels.description: The share of time the busiest server is currently spending paused for Java garbage collection. Sustained high values mean the JVM is under memory pressure and can add latency to transactions.
panels.title: GC

panels.description: Whether the cluster is currently rebalancing partitions, for example after adding or removing a node. Shows IN PROGRESS while data is being moved between servers, otherwise NONE.
panels.title: Rebalance

panels.description: The rate of stored-procedure executions the cluster is running per second - the headline measure of how busy the database is. In a K-safe cluster each transaction fans out to every copy of its partition, so this counts each transaction once per copy and runs higher than the client transaction rate.
panels.title: Transactions/s

panels.description: The rate of stored-procedure executions across the cluster. In a K-safe cluster each transaction also runs on every replica of its partition, so this fan-out makes the count higher than the number of transactions actually issued by clients.
panels.title: Procedure calls

panels.description: The number of transactions that were aborted or failed, counted once per client request - the errors your applications actually saw. Anything above zero points to application errors or problems the database hit while running transactions.
panels.title: Procedure errors

panels.description: The slowest single transaction seen recently, measured as initiator latency: from the moment the request arrives on the network to the moment the response is sent back, including queueing, execution and, in a K-safe cluster, the wait for every copy of the partition to confirm. A high value flags an occasional slow transaction even when typical latency looks fine.
panels.title: Max Latency

panels.description: The rate at which rows are being successfully brought in through import connectors. Zero means no data is currently being imported.
panels.title: Import TPS

panels.description: The number of transactions that have been initiated but whose command-log record has not yet been written to disk. With synchronous command logging this is always zero; a growing value with asynchronous logging means logging is falling behind.
panels.title: Commandlog queue

panels.description: Transaction throughput over time, broken out per server. Counts procedure executions including the fan-out to partition replicas in a K-safe cluster, so totals run above the client-issued transaction rate. Use it to see the workload trend and whether load is spread evenly across the cluster.
panels.title: Transaction rate

panels.description: The 99.9th-percentile initiator latency per server: the full request-to-response time, including queueing, execution and, in a K-safe cluster, the wait for all partition copies to confirm. It shows the worst latency all but the slowest 0.1% of transactions stay under, so it surfaces occasional stalls.
panels.title: 999th percentile request execution time (whole transaction path)

panels.description: The slowest execution time recorded for each stored procedure, timing only the procedure's own work - queueing, network, and the wait for partition replicas are not included. Use it to find which procedures are the most expensive; compare with the initiator-latency panels to see how much overhead the full transaction path adds.
panels.title: Max procedure execution time (just the procedure)

panels.description: The busiest server's CPU usage right now - the highest VoltDB CPU percentage across all servers. A high value here points to a single overloaded node even when the rest of the cluster is fine.
panels.title: Max CPU Usage

panels.description: The most memory-stressed server in the cluster: the largest share of a server's memory being used by VoltDB, as a percentage. It shows the single busiest server (not a cluster average) so one hot node isn't hidden. Use the Memory dashboard for a per-server breakdown.
panels.title: Worst RAM usage

panels.description: The server closest to its Java memory limit: the largest share of the available Java heap in use across all servers, as a percentage. Values near 100% risk pauses or out-of-memory errors. Use the Memory dashboard for per-server detail.
panels.title: Worst heap usage

panels.description: CPU used by each server's VoltDB process over time, from 0 to 100%. This is the database process only, not the whole machine, so it shows how hard VoltDB itself is working on each node.
panels.title: CPU Usage

panels.description: The total physical memory (RAM) the VoltDB process is using on each server. Steady growth toward the machine's memory limit risks swapping or the process being killed.
panels.title: RSS size

panels.description: The Java heap memory in use by VoltDB on each server. Watch for values climbing toward the configured heap limit, which can cause long GC pauses or out-of-memory errors.
panels.title: Java Heap Memory Usage

panels.description: The number of client connections currently open on each server, shown against the configured connection limit. As the open count approaches the limit, the server is at risk of refusing new clients.
panels.title: Client connections

panels.description: The rate at which each server is accepting new client connections. Sudden spikes can indicate clients reconnecting repeatedly rather than holding steady connections.
panels.title: Connections accepted

panels.description: The rate at which each server is refusing new connections because it has reached its connection limit. Any sustained value here means clients are actively being turned away.
panels.title: Connections dropped per second

panels.description: The number of file descriptors each server currently has open. Compare against the file-descriptor limit; a count climbing toward it warns of exhaustion that would break connections and file operations.
panels.title: Open file descriptors

panels.description: The number of completed transaction results waiting to be sent back to clients on each server. A growing backlog means the server is producing results faster than clients are reading them.
panels.title: Finished Transactions VoltDB is about to send back to the client

panels.description: The rate of requests arriving from each connected client host. Use it to see which clients are driving the most load on the cluster.
panels.title: Client transaction rate by connected host

panels.description: The current clock difference between each pair of servers in the cluster, laid out as a grid. Large values point to a specific node whose clock has drifted and may need its time service checked.
panels.title: Clock skew matrix (current)

panels.description: The largest clock difference seen between each pair of servers over the selected time range. It highlights nodes whose clocks drifted at any point in the window, even if they are aligned again now.
panels.title: Clock skew matrix (worst in selected time range)

panels.description: The total time spent paused for Java garbage collection across the cluster over the selected time range. Large totals mean the JVMs are spending significant time reclaiming memory instead of running transactions.
panels.title: Total GC time

panels.description: The share of time each server spends in young-generation garbage collection, which is short and frequent. Some activity here is normal; steadily rising values indicate growing memory churn.
panels.title: New Gen GC Time

panels.description: How often young-generation garbage collection runs per second on each server. Frequent short collections are normal, but a sharp rise signals the JVM is allocating memory rapidly.
panels.title: New Gen GC Count

panels.description: The share of time each server spends in old-generation garbage collection, which is less frequent but far more expensive and can pause the server. Sustained activity here often precedes long stalls.
panels.title: Old Gen GC Time

panels.description: How often old-generation garbage collection runs per second on each server. Repeated old-generation collections indicate heap pressure and usually mean the server is close to its memory limit.
panels.title: Old Gen GC Count

panels.description: A timeline showing when the cluster was rebalancing partitions. Use it to confirm whether a rebalance was running during a period of degraded performance.
panels.title: Rebalance history

panels.description: Details of recent partition rebalancing operations: how many rows and how much data were moved, progress, and timing. Rebalancing runs in segments, so the average figures shown are averages across those segments.
panels.title: Recent rebalances

panels.description: How often command logging fell so far behind that it had to pause transactions. Any value above zero means writes to the command log couldn't keep up, usually because the disk holding it is slow or saturated. Applies only when command logging runs in asynchronous mode.
panels.title: Command log backpressure

panels.description: When command logging last had to pause transactions to catch up. Shows a placeholder if it never has.
panels.title: Last backpressure

panels.description: How long it takes to create a new command-log file on disk (99th percentile). Rising times point to a slow or busy disk holding the command log.
panels.title: Command log segment allocation time (p99)
